READING

**The environmental baseline**

The strongroom runs at 62 per cent RH with an 11-point annual swing. The target is 45–55 per cent with a swing under 5 points. The gap is not marginal: 62 per cent is well into the range that accelerates hydrolysis in iron gall ink and in acidic board, and an 11-point swing means repeated dimensional cycling of the paper fibres. 2,900 of the 4,200 items are on one or both of those vulnerable supports, so most of the collection is being actively harmed every day the environment is uncorrected.

**What the deterioration data tells us**

Unusable items: 640 in 2019, 1,010 in 2025. That is 370 items lost over six years, or roughly 62 a year as stated. The trajectory is not flattening. By the time LINDCASTER treatment could reach its 1,360th item—at 70 items a month starting eight weeks after order, so roughly 20 months of work, finishing around mid-2028—the strongroom will have pushed perhaps another 100 items into the unusable band on top of the 1,010 already there.

**The conservator's written opinion**

This is the single most important piece of evidence in the file. Idris Sankey-Marchmont states in writing that rehousing and aqueous treatment carried out into the strongroom as it stands will need to be repeated within a decade. That is not a caveat buried in a footnote; it is the professional judgment of the person responsible for the collection's physical welfare, and it applies directly to every item that would be treated under LINDCASTER. It means that the GBP 340,000 spent under LINDCASTER does not buy permanent benefit: it buys roughly a decade's deferral of the same expenditure, after which the items are back in a damaging environment and the money is gone.

**The buffered-enclosure argument examined**

LINDCASTER relies on the claim that buffered enclosures hold an item's microclimate within 3 points of its packing condition for eight to twelve years. That is true, but it requires careful reading. The enclosures hold within 3 points of *packing condition*—not of the target standard. If an item is packed at 62 per cent, the enclosure holds it at roughly 59–65 per cent. That is still far above the 45–55 per cent standard and well within the range driving acid hydrolysis in iron gall ink. The enclosures buffer the *swing* better than they buffer the *level*, and it is the sustained high level that does chronic chemical damage to these supports. The microclimate benefit is real but partial, and the conservator's ten-year repeat-treatment finding already accounts for it.

**The 2029–30 capital risk**

LINDCASTER's viability as a long-term strategy depends on the GBP 400,000 unallocated line in the 2029–30 capital programme being awarded to the plant. Several things should give pause here. First, it is unallocated: the board sets it in November 2028 and nothing is committed against it. Second, by 2029–30 the Threlkeld quote (GBP 295,000, quoted June 2026) will be three to four years old; plant costs are not static and a revised quote could be higher. Third, if the capital is not awarded, the institution is left with: conservation work the conservator says needs repeating, no functioning environment, no bequest money, and no obvious alternative funding path. That is the worst-case outcome of LINDCASTER and it is not implausible. The probability of a committed capital line materialising from a board that has not yet set its 2029–30 programme is unknown; the risk is real.

Conversely, if HAVERSHOLT is chosen and the plant is installed, the 2029–30 capital line—if awarded—can go entirely to conservation, purchasing permanent treatment of perhaps 1,600 items in a controlled environment. That is a better outcome than LINDCASTER's 1,360 items in a bad environment plus an uncertain plant.

**Procurement timing under HAVERSHOLT**

The Threlkeld quote is held to 2027-01-30. Commissioning is 2027-05-29. The order must be placed fourteen weeks before commissioning, which calculates to approximately 2027-02-18. Ordering on or before 2027-01-30 (the quote's expiry) gives seventeen weeks of lead time, which exceeds the fourteen-week minimum. The institution has until the end of January 2027—five months from today—to place the order. That is a manageable window for a decision of this size.

Conservation under HAVERSHOLT can start within eight weeks of an order placed now or shortly after the plant decision is settled. At 70 items a month the GBP 45,000 (180 items) would be complete in about two and a half months of work, likely finishing before the plant is commissioned. Those 180 items will then sit in a corrected environment.

**Scale of protection compared**

LINDCASTER: 1,360 items get temporary treatment; 2,840 items get nothing active; the environment harms all 4,200 throughout; the conservator says the treatment must be repeated.

HAVERSHOLT: 180 items get durable treatment; all 4,200 items move into a controlled environment from May 2027; future conservation of any item, funded from any future budget, achieves permanent rather than temporary benefit; the conservator's written concern is addressed at root.

The apparent advantage of LINDCASTER—treating 1,360 rather than 180 items—dissolves once the temporary nature of that treatment is factored in. Treating 1,360 items in a way that needs redoing is not the same as durably treating 1,360 items.

**The bequest intent**

The Hesketh-Ravenna bequest is for the collection. Spending it on work that the conservator says will need repeating is poor stewardship of a one-time capital gift. Spending it on infrastructure that stops the clock for all 4,200 items and makes every future conservation pound worth a full pound rather than a fraction of one is a more defensible use of an unrepeatable resource.

**Conclusion**

HAVERSHOLT is the sounder course. It is more expensive in the short term for conservation throughput but it is the only option that addresses the cause rather than the symptoms, honours the conservator's professional judgment, eliminates the dependency on an uncommitted future capital line, and ensures that nothing commissioned now has to be commissioned again.

---

READING
  The conservator's written opinion that treatment in the current environment must be repeated within a decade is decisive, because it renders LINDCASTER's GBP 340,000 spend temporary rather than durable; HAVERSHOLT fixes the environment for all 4,200 items within the spending window, eliminates the repeat-treatment liability, and leaves the 2029–30 capital line free for conservation rather than plant; the 2029–30 line is unallocated and uncommitted, making LINDCASTER's long-term viability dependent on a board decision that has not been made and may not go in the collection's favour; and although HAVERSHOLT treats only 180 items actively, every future conservation pound spent in a corrected environment achieves permanent benefit rather than a decade-long deferral.

CALL
  HAVERSHOLT

GROUNDS
  The conservator's written finding that treatment in the present environment must be repeated within a decade makes LINDCASTER's entire GBP 340,000 a temporary measure rather than a permanent one, while HAVERSHOLT corrects the root cause for all 4,200 items within the spending window and removes the dependency on an uncommitted future capital line.
